signals.title: Introducing eve 1.0
signals.excerpt:
Published: November 17, 2026 | Authors: Andrew Barba, Shar Dara, Casey Gowrie, Colton Padden, Rui Conti, Ben Pankow, Owen Kephart, Murat Sutunc, Chad Hietala | Category: Company News

---

Today we're announcing eve 1.0, the open-source framework for building production-ready agents.

Since the public preview in June, we've worked with early adopters to prepare eve for 1.0, shipping 230+ releases and merging thousands of pull requests. With this release, eve is now generally available.

We've made eve faster, expanded integrations, and improved observability. Security controls let you decide which actions need approval and what data gets collected. We've also made it easier for coding agents to build with, measuring that experience with a rigorous evaluation suite.

With eve handling your harness and infrastructure, you and your agent can focus on building instead.

## Build production agents on a harness you own

The harness in eve is the loop that calls models, runs tools, and delegates work to subagents. You choose the model, add or replace tools, edit instructions, and decide which actions need approval. The open-source Workflow SDK saves progress as the agent runs, so it can pick up from its last completed step after a crash. Multiplayer sessions and agent-to-agent calls are built in.

For managed hosting, deploy your eve agent to Vercel. Vercel Workflows handles durable execution, and Vercel Sandbox runs agent-generated code in isolation.

Build software factories that turn requests into tested pull requests, company brains that answer questions from your business data, or customer-facing agents in your product.

...

## Give agents memory across sessions

We added native memory so agents can carry context from one session to the next. You choose the memory's scope and can use the built-in file memory, a memory provider, or one you build yourself.

Built-in `fileMemory` keeps data in memory in `eve dev` and in a private Vercel Blob store you configure on Vercel.

Other providers include claude-mem, Hindsight, Kybernesis Arcana, Memanto, memco, Supermemory, and Upstash AgentKit.

signals.title: Amazon S3 Vectors now supports hybrid search combining vector and full text for more relevant search results - AWS
signals.excerpt:
Amazon S3 Vectors now supports hybrid search that combines vector similarity search with full-text search within a single query. By combining semantic meaning and exact term matching into a single ranked list of results, hybrid search captures both intent and precise terms for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), agent memory, and search applications. This can deliver more relevant ranked results than either method alone. Hybrid search works with the same S3 Vectors APIs and maintains subsecond latency for infrequent queries and latency around 100 milliseconds or less for frequent queries.

S3 Vectors is designed to provide the same elasticity, durability, and availability as Amazon S3, and it reduces the total costs of storing and querying vectors by up to 90% compared to alternative vector solutions. With hybrid search, customers can now store the data that they want to make full-text searchable alongside the vectors. Customers write data with the PutVectors API as they do today and include the searchable text as another metadata field. S3 Vectors then automatically indexes that field for full-text search with BM25 relevance scoring. By default, S3 Vectors uses a language-agnostic text analyzer to index this data which works across most languages, and customers can optionally select a language-specific analyzer for more accurate language-aware matching. To perform a hybrid query, customers send their query text strings alongside their query vector in a single QueryVectors call; S3 Vectors runs both a vector search and a full-text search, fuses the two with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), and returns a single ranked list of the top K requested results. Customers can also run full-text and vector queries separately to apply own ranking logic, search across multiple text fields in a single query, and enable full-text search on existing data in place.

Hybrid search is available today in all commercial AWS Regions where Amazon S3 Vectors is available, and in the AWS China Regions.

signals.title: Hugging Face describes CQ quantization and GCMP adapters · Tensor Journal
signals.excerpt:
Hugging Face reports the CQ base scores 0.65 on GSM8K in company-reported results, and says it shows no significant difference from BF16. Its CQ + LoRA run is still in progress.

By Elena Voss

Published Nov 16, 2026 2 min read

Tensor Journal

## Key facts

Organization

Hugging Face

Other

Nov 14, 2026

huggingface.co

Hugging Face says it describes CQ, a calibration-free quantization format, and GCMP, a parameter-efficient adapter positioned as a replacement for LoRA. The material is dated November 14, 2026.

Hugging Face says CQ needs no calibration data. Its input is a Hugging Face checkpoint, and it runs layer by layer. The post says GCMP is compatible with CQ, NF4 and full-precision bases.

Hugging Face lists the CQ model at 18 GB and the NF4 model at 22.4 GB.

The benchmark model is Qwen3.8-27B. In company-reported results, the CQ base scores 0.65 on GSM8K. Hugging Face says CQ shows no significant difference from BF16 across all benchmarks. It reports an NF4 loss of 12.0 points on GSM8K against BF16. Hugging Face gives the benchmark size as 200–1,140 questions per task.

The post reports mean KL divergence on WikiText-2 of 0.0282 for CQ against BF16, and 0.033 for NF4 against BF16.

On Qwen3.8-27B, GCMP has 2.9M parameters, and its adapter is about 11 MB on disk. LoRA at rank thirty-two has about 159M trainable parameters and occupies about 320 MB on disk.

The adapter runs used the Alpaca dataset and a fixed set of training settings, covering steps, batch size, sequence length, learning rate and random seed. Hugging Face says those settings were identical across the compared runs.

Hugging Face reports that, on an NF4 base, GCMP scored 4.0 points higher on GSM8K (p = 0.04) than LoRA.

On ARC-Challenge, Hugging Face reports that CQ with GCMP was lower on ARC-Challenge (−4.2, p = 0.001) than NF4 with GCMP.

Hugging Face says the CQ + LoRA run is still in progress. The first CQ + LoRA adapter it evaluated came from an older trainer version, which the post describes as broken.

Hugging Face reports that CQ trainer step time fell from 27.6 seconds per step before a recent improvement to 8.6 seconds now.

Hugging Face says vLLM serving of GCMP currently requires a CQ base, while GCMP adapters on full-precision models run in Transformers for now. CQ supports pipeline parallelism across GPUs, but tensor parallelism is not yet supported. The post gives a per-token adapter routing buffer in vLLM of ~1 MB.

The CUDA kernels ship compiled. Hugging Face says they include a license check and are free during early access.

signals.title: OpenRouter Now Powers Inference on Hugging Face
signals.excerpt:
Sasha Blumenfeld · 11/16/2026

We built OpenRouter so developers can reach many models and providers through one API, use the best model for each task, and count on it to respond. Starting today, that extends to everyone building on Hugging Face. Chat models on Hugging Face Inference Providers now run through OpenRouter, with the same routing across providers that OpenRouter customers already rely on.

The integration also runs the other way. OpenRouter can now send a trace of each request to a Hugging Face Storage Bucket you own, so the prompts and responses from your real traffic sit next to the models and datasets you would use to evaluate or fine-tune on them. The setup guide has the steps.

## What you get on Hugging Face

Many chat models on Hugging Face are served by more than one provider. OpenRouter’s provider routing now powers routing on Hugging Face Inference Providers, and it picks the provider for each request based on live price, speed, and reliability. You don’t have to set anything up, and your existing Hugging Face token and code keep working.

You also get automatic failover. If a provider slows down or starts failing, requests go to other providers until it recovers. If a provider returns an error, the request is retried on the next one inside the same call.

When we rebuilt this routing in October, a live experiment measured 46% fewer requests hitting a capacity error, 16.9% faster time to first token, and 16.3% higher throughput, for 6.0% higher cost per request. Everyone building on Hugging Face now gets the same routing.

You stay in control of the trade-off. Adding a suffix to the model ID, such as `:fastest`, `:cheapest`, or a provider name, tells OpenRouter what to prioritize, and requests work through OpenAI’s Chat Completions and Responses APIs or Anthropic’s Messages API. A conversation also stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache.

Each model page has a new Providers tab with live price, speed, and uptime for every provider. You can see your spend by provider and turn off any provider you don’t want to use.

160 models from 38 labs are available this way today, which is every model OpenRouter serves that has a page on the Hub. They include the open-weight models developers use most on OpenRouter, where open-weight models carried about 70% of paid tokens in October:

- DeepSeek V4.1 Flash

signals.title: New Research Challenges GPU Utilization as Measure of Inference Infrastructure
signals.excerpt:
WEKA 

Nov 16, 2026, 09:00 ET

New NAND Research report underscores that busy GPUs aren't an accurate measure of productive output; introduces new Inference Economics Scorecard to measure inference infrastructure by the useful work it delivers, as applied in an eight-hour benchmark with Nebius on NVIDIA HGX B300 GPUs and WEKA NeuralMesh.

CHICAGO, Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- From Supercomputing 2026: WEKA, the AI data and memory infrastructure company, in collaboration with market intelligence firm NAND Research, today introduced the Inference Economics Scorecard, a new common framework for measuring inference infrastructure productivity and economic value by the useful work it delivers rather than by how busy it keeps GPUs. The scorecard defines nine measures, including tokens per watt, cost per inference, and context retention. It sets four testing rules, including runs of at least eight hours and counting only successful output. Already applied in a benchmark with Nebius, the AI cloud company, it comes as inference is claiming a growing share of AI infrastructure spending and buyers hit power, memory, and rack-space limits.

 

The New Math of Inference

Buyers Are Already Treating Inference Differently, New Research Finds New research from 451 Research by S&P Global shows organizations are already adapting, projecting that inference will grow from 34% of AI infrastructure spending in 2026 to 46% by 2030 and finding that 41% of organizations running inference buy fundamentally different infrastructure for it than for the rest of their IT stack.

...

Why GPU Utilization Falls Short for Inference

For years, training was the dominant AI workload. Because training keeps GPUs busy with large, predictable jobs, GPU utilization became the default measure of AI infrastructure productivity. Inference, especially agentic inference, places very different demands on GPUs. An agent does not simply answer a prompt; it completes a task over many steps, and at each step it re-reads the context it built earlier. After the GPU evicts that context from memory to make room for other users and sessions, it must recompute it when the task returns, and the task makes no further progress until that work is done. The result is a GPU that is fully utilized but unproductive because it wastes cycles recomputing the same tokens multiple times.

The Inference Economics Scorecard measures inference systems at production scale: completed requests across many concurrent users, sustained over hours rather than minutes.

"The industry has been grading inference with a training-era report card. GPU utilization tells you the chip was busy. It cannot tell you whether the work was finished, repeated, or thrown away, and with agents, a lot of it is repeated," said Liran Zvibel, co-founder and CEO of WEKA. "Power, supply, and rack space are constraints now as much as capital. The new math required for inference infrastructure is useful work per watt, per rack, per dollar, at the response times your users expect. The Inference Economics Scorecard puts that math on paper, and WEKA will be measured by it like everyone else."

From Busy to Productive: How the Scorecard Works The Inference Economics Scorecard defines nine measures of inference performance and economics: tokens per watt, tokens per rack, cost per inference, GPU goodput, time to first token and end-to-end latency, memory efficiency, operational density, agent concurrency, and context retention. It also sets the discipline for testing against them:

- The same workload and service targets across every system tested
- Measurement of the whole serving stack
- Runs of at least eight hours
- Only successful output counted

"The most expensive mistake in AI infrastructure right now is buying for peak throughput and paying for repeated work," said Steve McDowell, principal analyst and founder at NAND Research. "Agentic workloads make that mistake easy to miss, because every step of a long task re-reads context that a busy GPU may have to rebuild from scratch. We designed the scorecard so buyers can hold any system to the same standard: finished work, measured over hours, with every failure counted. The Nebius benchmark shows what that discipline reveals, because it ran for the full eight hours and counted every request that failed or timed out."

Putting It to the Test: Real Agent Load, Sustained for Eight Hours WEKA and Nebius recently applied the scorecard's rules in a joint benchmark on NVIDIA HGX B300 systems and reported results on several measures. The test ran on one eight-GPU node serving DeepSeek-V4-Pro to 512 active sessions drawn from a corpus of more than 5,000 real agentic coding sessions over eight hours per configuration, counting every failed and timed-out request.

Using WEKA NeuralMesh with Augmented Memory Grid, which pools NVMe across the cluster as a shared context tier, the node produced 3.7x the output tokens per GPU-hour compared with HBM-only serving on the same GPUs, and 97% of successfully completed requests reached a first token within five seconds, up from 44%. On HBM-only serving, 60% of prefill work was recomputed from context the cluster had already processed earlier in the session; with Augmented Memory Grid, 6.8%. At the measured rate, the HBM-only node would need about 30 hours to produce what Augmented Memory Grid produced in eight. The full benchmark is published at weka.io and nebius.com blogs.

"Peak throughput shows what a system can do for a few minutes, but our customers run agents for hours, days, or longer, so what matters is sustained useful work," said Narek Tatevosyan, Vice President of Product at Nebius. "Over a full shift, the HBM-only configuration steadily lost ground as context fell out of memory and timeouts climbed, while WEKA NeuralMesh kept first-token latency flat the entire run. That

...

Reproducible by Design: Open Traces and Tooling The traces and tooling behind the benchmark are open-sourced so anyone can run the same workload on their own systems and compare results on equal terms. Because the traces come from real agentic coding sessions rather than synthetic load, and include the varied timing and complexity of real work, they give any team a realistic stand-in for production. Others are already building on them: SemiAnalysis's AgentX benchmark is built on the traces, and NVIDIA AIPerf benchmarking tool ships a loader for them.

Table 1. Performance per GPU of Vera Rubin NVL72 relative to GB300 NVL72, MLPerf Training v6.1, closed division

...

## DeepSeek-V3 671B: 2x per GPU on the hardest workload

DeepSeek-V3 671B is a 671-billion-parameter token-dropless Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model and the most demanding workload in the suite. Expert parallelism turns every iteration into a burst of all-to-all communication, so fabric efficiency shows up directly in time to train.

Vera Rubin NVL72 trained the benchmark in 4.14 minutes using 1,024 GPUs across 16 racks. GB300 NVL72 ran the identical 1,024-GPU configuration in 8.03 minutes, close to 2x per GPU, and the largest generational improvement in this round. Halving time to train roughly doubles how many experiments a team can run in a quarter, and experiment throughput is what moves model quality. 

At a larger scale, GB300 NVL72 produced the fastest absolute result of the round: 1.38 minutes across 10,240 GPUs. That is one training job spread across 160 racks, each its own NVLink domain, and it shows the platform’s scale-out fabric holding up long after the job outgrows a single rack.

## Post-training arrives, and Vera Rubin leads it

MLPerf Training v6.1 adds its first agentic LLM reinforcement learning post-training benchmark, Qwen 3.5 397B GRPO, reflecting a fundamental shift in AI development. Post-training has emerged as the critical differentiator for agentic accuracy, making the GRPO workload uniquely demanding. The continuous cycle of generating rollouts, scoring them, and updating weights pushes system architectures to their limits by forcing constant, massive weight migrations between inference and training engines.

Vera Rubin NVL72 achieved the fastest time for this new benchmark with a time of 10.44 minutes at 1,024 GPUs (6.1-0117), compared with 13.78 minutes for GB300 NVL72 (6.1-0031) at the same scale. The Vera Rubin platform also proved its flexibility by submitting on two different inference backends: NVIDIA NeMo RL with TensorRT-LLM at 10.44 minutes and with vLLM at 10.94 minutes (6.1-0118). Shipping two viable inference backends on a benchmark this new says as much about software maturity as it does about silicon.

Teaching these models to observe, reason, and act requires running each rollout in a simulated environment and executing tool calls, code, or API validations. Because driving these simulations is intensely CPU-bound, the NVIDIA Vera CPU is integral to the architecture, sustaining more than 22,500 concurrent RL environments across 256 CPUs in a single Vera CPU rack. 

While the GPUs handle massive token generation and rapid weight updates, the Vera CPUs work in lockstep to simulate the environments, ensuring the accelerators are continuously fed with the rich feedback required to perfect agentic workflows.

signals.title: Neo4j releases Relate, an open source in-memory database built for AI agents
signals.excerpt:
Mon 16 Nov 2026 · First reported by Cyprus Shipping News

...

- Relate is open source under the Apache 2.0 license and built in Rust
- It runs in-process, in memory, with optional disk storage for durability
- It includes an MCP server, a command-line tool, and Bolt and HTTP query endpoints
- Errors carry retryable flags, and a row cap stops large results from flooding an agent

...

One caveat up front: the article is based on a company release, distributed through Business Wire. The performance figures are the vendor's own, and the source gives no independent benchmarks or pricing details.

...

Most of the announcement is about small design choices that reflect how agents fail and recover. Relate detects when an agent harness, the software wrapper that runs an agent, is calling it. When something goes wrong, it returns structured errors with an explicit flag saying whether retrying makes sense. Neo4j says this lets an agent correct itself without custom code to interpret error text.

Another choice limits how much comes back. Relate caps the number of rows in a result and adds a marker showing the result was cut short. The point is to avoid overfilling an agent's context window, the limited amount of text a model can consider at once. Agents then receive results of a predictable size.

Connectivity comes built in. Relate has a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, a common standard for letting agents use outside tools, plus a command-line tool. It also exposes Bolt and HTTP Query API v2 endpoints, so existing graph drivers, orchestration frameworks and developer tools should work with it.

## Graph queries and retrieval

Relate supports Cypher, the query language Neo4j uses for graph data. A single Cypher statement can search by vector similarity, which finds items with similar meaning, and follow connections through the graph in the same step. Neo4j says this supports multi-hop reasoning, where an answer depends on following several links in a row, and GraphRAG, which feeds a model facts drawn from a graph. The company says this gives agents more accurate results and fewer hallucinations, meaning invented answers. That claim is Neo4j's and is not tested in the source.

The release says Relate is 100% openCypher compliant and more than 97% compliant with GQL, the standard graph query language. Those numbers suggest queries written for other graph systems may carry over, though the source does not say how that was measured. It is released under the Apache 2.0 license, a permissive open source license.

signals.title: NVIDIA Releases Qwen3.8-Flash-Next Experimental Checkpoint :: Neural Wire
signals.excerpt:
### Experimental Mixed-Precision Checkpoint Released for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next

NVIDIA has released an experimental mixed-precision Quantization-Aware Deployment (QAD) checkpoint for the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next model. According to the model card documentation, the release, identified as `nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4-QAD`, is intended for testing purposes and utilizes mixed-precision techniques.

The release has prompted technical discussion within developer communities, specifically on Reddit, regarding its efficiency compared to existing quantized versions of the model.

### Technical Comparisons and Performance Observations

Early assessments from independent developers suggest that the experimental checkpoint may face competition from existing optimized versions. Specifically, users on Reddit have noted that the `nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP4-Local` variant appears to offer superior performance characteristics for certain hardware configurations.

Technical observations shared by community members highlight several key differences in quantization strategies:

- Memory Efficiency: The `FP4-Local` version reportedly utilizes NVFP4 and MXFP8 more broadly, alongside CSF-compressed scaling factors. These optimizations are estimated to reduce the model size by approximately 3GB.
- Hardware Throughput: On professional-grade hardware, such as the RTX PRO 6000, users have reported that the `FP4-Local` variant allows for a token pool of approximately 1 million tokens, which is double the capacity of the ~130GB NVFP4 models. Additionally, the `FP4-Local` version is noted for providing higher throughput per request.
- Quantization Methods: While the experimental checkpoint uses mixed-precision QAD, other versions, such as those released by RadixArk, utilize a method where only the experts are quantized to NVFP4, borrowing FP8 PLE parameters from the original Qwen FP8 checkpoint.

Some developers have expressed skepticism regarding the utility of the new experimental checkpoint, noting that it appears significantly larger and slower than the `FP4-Local` alternative without providing immediate, obvious gains in performance or efficiency.

November 16, 2026

Tencent today announced the release of Hy4 flash, the latest addition to its Hy model family. Hy4 flash has 224 billion total parameters (including 64 billion Engram parameters) with only 12 billion active parameters, and supports multimodal inputs and a context length of up to 1M tokens. It is the most cost-effective Hy model to date, priced at approximately US$0.070 per million input tokens, US$0.281 per million output tokens, and US$0.003 per million cached input tokens — a substantial reduction from Hy4.

Hy4 flash vs Hy4 API Price Comparison in USD (https://hy.tencent.ai/research/hy4-flash)

To achieve this level of cost performance while maintaining strong intelligence and practical utility, the Tencent Hy team made a series of engineering choices across the model pipeline:

signals.title: Building a Private AI Document Assistant on an 8GB GPU Using RAG and llama.cpp
signals.excerpt:
## A smaller GPU needs a smaller question, not a smaller ambition

In Part 1, I explored the practical options for running quantized language models on limited GPU memory. Part 2 narrowed the discussion to Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with llama.cpp. It treated the memory budget and latency as things to inspect, not performance numbers to promise. The experiment separated prompt processing from generation, explained the KV cache, and used a fixed configuration that readers could reproduce.

The obvious next question is whether that model can do useful work. Asking it to summarize its own knowledge is easy enough. Asking it to answer a question about an internal project report is different. That report may not exist anywhere in its training data, and sending the entire document into a 4,096-token context is wasteful even if it technically fits. If a team changes a release date on Monday, the assistant needs to follow the new document, not its old guess.

That is where retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, becomes useful. RAG does not retrain the model. It finds passages that might answer the question, puts only those passages into the prompt, and asks the local model to reason from that evidence. The model still can make mistakes. But now we have specific places to investigate when an answer is incomplete: extraction, chunking, retrieval, prompt construction, or generation.

The application in this article is intentionally modest. You can index a folder of text-based PDFs, Markdown files, and text files. You can ask a question from the command line. The assistant prints an answer, shows the source passages it supplied to the model, and reports where the time went. A separate script runs fixed questions repeatedly so a configuration change can be checked against the same workload.

This is not an attempt to squeeze a second model into the remaining GPU memory. It is an attempt to spend the GPU memory on the one model that really needs it.

## The architecture: one GPU model, two CPU components

The application has an ingestion path and a question-answering path. Those are different operations and should be measured separately.

> INDEXING (runs when documents change)

```plain
PDF / TXT / Markdown
| PyMuPDF or text reader
v
Page-aware text excerpts
| 160-word chunks, 32-word overlap
v
CPU Sentence Transformer embeddings
| normalized float32 vectors
v
FAISS IndexFlatIP + source metadata (local disk)

QUESTION ANSWERING (runs for each question)
User question
| CPU query embedding
v
FAISS top-k vector search
| filenames, pages, excerpt IDs
v
Token-budget check using llama-server
| evidence + question + system rules
v
Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct Q4_K_M via llama.cpp
| local HTTP, 127.0.0.1
v
Answer + source pointers + latency record

```

Local RAG architecture showing CPU-based document indexing, FAISS retrieval, and GPU-accelerated LLM inference with source citations.

Create a simple two-lane architecture diagram, not a stock illustration. Use blue for offline indexing, green for question-time retrieval, and a single GPU box for inference. Suggested alt text: “Architecture of a CPU-indexed RAG pipeline with llama.cpp running generation on an 8GB GPU.”

The separation matters because a small embedding model does not need to consume the GPU's precious VRAM. For this tutorial, `sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2` runs explicitly on the CPU. FAISS also runs on the CPU. The larger Qwen model runs behind `llama-server` with the GPU backend. The embeddings and index use ordinary system RAM, while the GPU remains available for the language model and its KV cache.

There is a trade-off. CPU embeddings may be slower during initial indexing, particularly for a large collection. But ingestion is normally less time-sensitive than interactive generation. For a personal document folder, predictable GPU headroom can be more valuable than a few seconds saved during indexing. If you eventually need to index millions of chunks, you should revisit the retrieval system; this tutorial is a baseline, not an architecture for every scale.

...

The indexer records each passage's relative filename, page number, and chunk ID. Those are deliberately simple identifiers. A sentence from page five of an operations manual should not become an anonymous vector that cannot be traced back to its origin. Markdown and TXT files use page number one because they have no native pagination. If you need heading-level citations, extend the metadata later.

I use chunks of 160 whitespace-delimited words with a 32-word overlap. These are words, not model tokens; treating them as equivalent would be a mistake. The chunk size is just the extraction setting. The final question-time prompt must be checked with the language model's actual tokenizer. Overlap makes it less likely that a critical sentence is cut in half, although it also duplicates text and can return repetitive evidence. There is no universal correct chunk size. Test it on your documents.

The program stores the vectors in a FAISS `IndexFlatIP` index. Each embedding is L2-normalized before indexing and each question embedding is normalized before searching. With normalized vectors, inner product becomes cosine similarity. The returned similarity score is useful for ranking; it is not a probability that the answer is true. Do not invent a universal confidence threshold such as “0.8 means correct.” Calibrate decisions with a labelled evaluation set instead.

...

This reduces a class of prompt-injection mistakes, but prompting alone is not a security boundary.

In this implementation, the model has no email, network browsing, filesystem editing, or command-execution tool. That limits what a malicious document can cause the model to do.

signals.excerpt:
Nvidia uploaded Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4-QAD on Nov 17, 2026—a 180B image-text MoE with aggressive ModelOpt QAD mixing NVFP4 and MXFP8. How it differs from NVFP4.

Nov 17, 2026· 8 min read· Yash Thakker

NVIDIA on November 17, 2026 added a second public quantization experiment atop Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: `nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4-QAD`, an image-text-to-text mixture-of-experts checkpoint exported with ModelOpt QAD after 100 optimizer updates. It ships the full multimodal stack— vision encoder, PLE n-gram embedding, and MTP module—in roughly 129.7 GB of safetensors shards.

For local inference engineers, the important distinction is naming: -QAD means quantization-aware training tweaks, not merely re-labeled NVFP4 weights. NVIDIA''s card warns the recipe is more aggressive than `Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` and that accuracy gains are not statistically established.

## TL;DR

| Item | Model card claim |
| --- | --- |
| Base model | Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next |
| Training stack | NVIDIA ModelOpt + NeMo AutoModel (FSDP2) |
| QAD steps | 100 optimizer updates |
| Expert precision | NVFP4 routed + shared experts (trained) |
| Extra layers | GDN / QSA / indexer projections → MXFP8 |
| Disk footprint | ~129.7 GB weights |
| HF task | image-text-to-text |

## What QAD changes in the weight stack

A model core split into matching shards for distribution, echoing consolidated NVFP4 and MXFP8 safetensors

The Hugging Face README includes a component table. Summarized:

- Main LM routed experts (48 MoE groups) stay NVFP4 block size 16, trained with QAD.
- Shared experts (144 linear matrices) move to NVFP4 under QAD—where the earlier NVFP4-only release left them differently.
- GDN projections (180 matrices) use MXFP8 blocks under QAD.

NVIDIA explicitly says the repository name''s -QAD suffix identifies the method, not a promise that the old NVFP4 recipe stayed intact.

Consolidation note: NVIDIA merged shards for distribution, verified SHA256 against export, and claims tensor names, shapes, dtypes, and values are unchanged—relevant if you diff against internal checkpoints.

## Hardware and deployment reality

...

explainx.ai previously covered Qwen3.8-Flash-Next FP4 on 96 GiB for workstation-class NVFP4 inference. This QAD drop is larger and experimental:

- Card metadata when fetched showed on the order of 180B parameters and ~130 GB files—plan multi-GPU or tensor-parallel serving.
- Pair with NVIDIA Rubin / DGX Spark SC26 news if you are standardizing on NVIDIA''s FP4 software path, but do not assume Spark-class 96 GiB holds the full multimodal artifact without offloading vision weights.

November 17, 2026

Sarvam has opened Sarvam Token Factory to everyone. Sarvam Token Factory is an inference platform from Sarvam that serves its own models and open-weight models from GPU clusters in India. Developers reach every model through one OpenAI-compatible API. For India-based teams, this means low-latency tokens without sending traffic to overseas clouds. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension.

## TL;DR

- Size: 8 models listed at launch, including Sarvam 105B (105B total, 9B active, 128K context), GLM 5.3, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, Kimi K3.1 Pro and Gemma 4 31B.
- Runs on: NVIDIA B200 clusters in India. Sarvam 105B now fits on 1 B200 per replica. On-premise deployment is offered to enterprises.
- Performance: Fastest first token from Mumbai on most tested cases, per Sarvam’s own measurements.
- Best: Kimi K3.1 Pro at 6,177 tokens/s per GPU vs 3,213 for InferenceX, at 70 tokens/s per user (1.9x).

...

It is a managed inference stack, not a single model. Sarvam ... The launch post lists 8 models: Sarvam 105B, GLM 5.3, GLM 5.3 Flash, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, Kimi K3.1 Pro and Gemma 4 31B.

The docs split them into 2 groups. Pay-as-you-go models run on shared endpoints. DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3.1 Pro, Qwen 3.8 27B, Clef and EmbeddingGemma 2 need Provisioned Throughput, enabled per organisation.

## How does it work?

The stack has 3 layers around a shared cache:

- Control plane: a cache-aware router, admission control and a planner.
- Inference engine: separate GPU pools for prefill and decode.
- Cache: GPU memory plus a shared G3 store built on Mooncake.

It builds on vLLM, SGLang, Dynamo, Mooncake, NIXL, DeepEP, DeepGEMM and FlashInfer. An orchestrator agent proposes experiments, and an engineer approves each deployment.

Caching drives most of the gains. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash serves 450B+ tokens per day, with 95.7% of prompt tokens served from cache. On GLM 5.3, the planner cut prefill GPU-hours from 32.3 to 17.1 under the same replayed load.

For Sarvam 105B, MXFP8 weights plus speculative decoding raised output throughput about 2.2x. That cut each replica from 2 B200s to 1. Sarvam says none of these changes reduced accuracy.

## How fast is it? Benchmarks

All numbers below come from Sarvam’s launch post. They are self-reported.

- Sarvam 105B: 0.2 s first token and 330 tokens/s for a single user.
- Gemma 4 31B (10K prompt, Mumbai): 0.40 s first token and 308 tokens/s, vs 2.00 s and 193 tokens/s at the only other provider.
- Kimi K3.1 Pro (16 B200s): 6,177 vs 3,213 tokens/s per GPU against InferenceX at 70 tokens/s per user.
- Heavy agent load (72 sessions): median first token 0.8 s vs 11.6 s for InferenceX.
- GLM 5.3 Flash (64 sessions): p99 first token 3.2 s vs 14.1 s for stock vLLM and Dynamo.

The results are not a clean sweep. On DeepSeek V4.1 Flash with a 10K prompt, Together posts 0.71 s first token vs Sarvam’s 0.90 s. Together also streams faster, at 278 tokens/s vs 130 on Sarvam Standard.

signals.title: Huawei open-sources MACaQ quantizer for running AI models locally
signals.excerpt:
INSIGHTEX Editorial Desk

NOV 15, 2026

Published by

INSIGHTEX Editorial Desk

Why it matters

For startups building on-device or self-hosted AI products, the speed and memory cost of quantization affect which hardware a deployment needs. If the stated figures hold up under independent testing, compressing a 122B-parameter model with 32.5 GB of memory could make large models more accessible to small teams. Compatibility with standard llama.cpp also keeps switching costs low for operators already using GGUF files.

## What happened

Huawei has released MACaQ, a quantization tool it had been using internally, as an open-source project built for local inference, according to the project's page on GitHub. The toolkit shrinks AI models that handle text, images, video and audio so they can run with llama.cpp, vLLM, Diffusers and PyTorch. It is distributed under the Apache License 2.0.

According to the project page, MACaQ quantized a 122B-parameter model in 64 minutes while using 32.5 GB of device memory. The page also says it delivers lower perplexity than the MR-GPTQ and DuQuant++ methods, or matches their best Llama-3-8B results while taking about one eleventh of the quantization time. Output formats include 2-, 3- and 4-bit GGUF files as well as W4A4 checkpoints.

A companion tool, MACaQ-R, reworks the weight codes inside existing GGUF models to raise their quality and tailor them to particular workloads. The resulting files still run on an unmodified llama.cpp installation. Separately, W4A4 kernels have been submitted as pull requests to the CANN software stack, although running complete models requires integration with an Ascend inference runtime.

## Context

The project measures itself against the MR-GPTQ and DuQuant++ methods. It also compares its output with previously published GGUF builds of Qwen3-4B, using file size and KL divergence relative to FP16. The team has published a research paper describing the method and has posted a MACaQ-R version of the Qwen3.6-35B-A3B mixture-of-experts model on Hugging Face.

signals.title: LongCat-2.5: Meituan open-sources a 1.6T agent model under MIT, trained and served without Nvidia · Harel Asaf
signals.excerpt:
Meituan's LongCat team released the weights for LongCat-2.5 this week under the MIT license, and the combination matters: a 1.6-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts with roughly 48B active parameters per token, native multimodality, a 512K-token context window, and agentic-coding benchmarks in Claude Opus 5 territory, trained and deployed without any Nvidia hardware. The weights landed on Hugging Face about a week after the model's official unveiling, alongside a quantized W4A4 variant and an NPU deployment recipe. This is now one of the strongest truly open models you can actually download, modify, and serve yourself, with the caveat that serving it takes a small data center. All benchmark and infrastructure numbers below come from the model card and are vendor-reported.

...

## The benchmarks, all vendor-reported

The model card's table compares LongCat-2.5 against LongCat-2.0 and frontier models including GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8 and Opus 5, GLM-5.3, Kimi K3, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. Numbers marked with an asterisk on the card are cited from external sources rather than run by the team, so treat cross-vendor comparisons with the usual care.

The highlights: Terminal-Bench v2.1 at 88.4, just under Opus 5's 89.1 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash's 90.6, and far above LongCat-2.0's 70.8. On the harder Terminal-Bench v4.0 the gap to Opus 5 widens, 38.5 to 53.9, and on Program Bench (Almost Resolved) it scores 25.5 against Opus 5's 37.0. PaperBench is a bright spot at 82.1, near the top of the table, and 3DCodeBench at 55.4 is the highest score listed. Against its own predecessor the jump is dramatic across the board: DeepSWE goes from 9.7 to 64.6, AutomationBench from 15.8 to 51.8, JobBench from 44.4 to 65.4.

The honest reading: this is a frontier-adjacent agent model that trades blows with the best on some evaluations and clearly trails Opus 5 on terminal-heavy work. For an open-weights model under MIT, that is a new watermark.

## Trained and served without Nvidia

The infrastructure section of the card is as interesting as the benchmarks. Training ran on domestic Chinese AI accelerators, and the team reports supernode-aware parallelism, sharding, and communication-computation overlap delivering 86% higher per-device throughput than a DDP baseline on long-sequence SFT tasks. The RL infrastructure keeps token log probabilities bitwise-identical across training, prefill, and decoding, which anyone who has debugged train-serve skew will appreciate, and KV cache work nearly doubled decode KV capacity without increasing TPOT on the tested workload.

The W4A4 quantization story is the deployment enabler: expert weights and activations go to native INT4 on domestic accelerators using FlatQuant-style learnable transformations, with accuracy the team says is comparable to the unquantized model on evaluated benchmarks. Against a W8A8 MoE baseline, online stress tests show 43.3% higher prefill throughput, 42.77% higher decode throughput, 15.91% lower TTFT, and 19.72% lower TPOT, with grouped GEMM kernels averaging 1.73x speedup. Combined with KV cache quantization, W4A4KV8 delivers 92% higher decode throughput than W8A8KV16. A separate W4A4 weight release is published alongside the main model.

## How to actually run it

Be realistic about the hardware. The reference NPU deployment, documented in the SGLang-FluentLLM repository, targets Huawei's Ascend Atlas A2 platform, and the sample configuration is a 194-card Atlas A2 Pod cluster with 16 cards per prefill/decode machine and 2 cards for the encoder. At 1.6T parameters even INT4 weights are in the hundreds of gigabytes, so this is a cluster model, not a laptop model. The deployment stack is CANN 9.0.0 with torch_npu and torchair matched to PyTorch 2.9.0, which tells you the software path is Huawei-first.

If you do not run Ascend hardware, the practical routes are the hosted API on the official LongCat platform, which sits behind a Meituan account login so I could not verify pricing without signing up, or waiting for community inference support. GPU-oriented serving stacks have not published verified LongCat-2.5 recipes at the time of writing, and I would not assume vLLM or stock SGLang handles the architecture without checking.

...

Vendor tables with asterisked competitor numbers are not independent evaluations, and several strong results here are self-run only. Do not assume the model is cheap to serve because it is efficient on Ascend: the reference deployment is a 194-card pod, and nothing about the release suggests single-node practicality. And the MIT license covers the weights, not the compute you would need to use them.

The DGX Spark Developer Kit changes how researchers work.

It scales from one system, or node, to four — linked directly to one another over NVIDIA ConnectX-7 networking, with no network switch to buy or set up. 

At four nodes, it provides 512GB of combined memory and 20TB of NVMe storage that provides researchers more capacity to distribute models and scientific workloads across the cluster. With NVFP4, researchers can deploy models with up to 700B parameters locally across the four DGX Spark clusters, such as DeepSeek V4.1.

With that much power at the desk, researchers with a fixed compute and server allocation no longer have to wait in a queue for every job. Teams can develop and debug on their own, saving server hours for production runs and keeping unpublished results, and proprietary datasets on premises.

...

- The Hartwig Group at UC Berkeley is using a DGX Spark to perform LoRA fine-tuning on the Nemotron 3 Super 120B-A12B model for chemistry machine learning, training a prediction head on experimental values. By running locally on the Spark using NVFP4 quantization, the lab successfully fit a 120B-class model on a single device and bypassed multi-day cluster queue times, allowing them to run continuous eight- to 24-hour training fits back-to-back.
